concept.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
concept.definition: An architecture in which a generative language model is conditioned on documents fetched by a retrieval system at inference time, combining parametric memory (model weights) with non-parametric memory (an external index). Introduced by Lewis et al. (2020) as a way to give seq2seq models explicit, updatable access to knowledge and provenance for their outputs.
concept.intuition: Instead of forcing the model to memorize everything, give it an open-book exam: look up the relevant passages first, then write the answer with those passages in front of it.
concept.mechanics: A query encoder embeds the input, a retriever finds the top-k nearest passages in a dense vector index, and the generator produces output conditioned on the input plus retrieved passages. The index can be updated with new documents without retraining the generator.
concept.formula: p(y|x) ≈ Σ_z p_eta(z|x) · p_theta(y|x,z), where the sum marginalizes over the top-k retrieved documents z; p_eta is the retriever distribution and p_theta is the generator distribution.
concept.failure_modes: Fails when retrieval returns irrelevant, stale, or poisoned documents, since the generator tends to trust its context; also degrades on questions requiring synthesis across many documents rather than lookup of one passage.
concept.misconceptions: RAG does not eliminate hallucination — models can ignore, misread, or over-trust retrieved context. It also does not make the model's parametric knowledge current; only the retrieved portion is up to date.
concept.example: A trading assistant asked 'What is the current CFTC position limit on WTI crude futures?' retrieves the relevant CME/CFTC rulebook passages and answers from them, citing the document, instead of relying on potentially outdated training data.

citations.source: Lewis et al., 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks' (NeurIPS 2020)
